title: Polymorphism
summary: One interface, many shapes — and the runtime mechanics (vtables, dynamic dispatch) and pitfalls behind making that actually work.

slides.markdown:
**Polymorphism** means the same call — `shape.area()` — behaves differently depending on the actual object it runs on, letting code written against one interface work correctly for many concrete types. It comes in three flavors: overriding (runtime), overloading (compile-time), and generics (parametric).

This topic covers how runtime polymorphism actually works under the hood (vtables), where it surprises people (overload resolution, constructors calling overridable methods), and why it's the mechanism behind the Open/Closed Principle.

slides.sectionTitle: Polymorphism defined: one interface, many shapes
slides.markdown:
**Polymorphism** ('many shapes') is the ability to call the same method name on different objects and get behavior appropriate to each object's actual type, without the caller needing to know which type it is. A loop calling `shape.area()` over a list of `Circle`, `Square`, and `Triangle` objects runs three different area formulas through one line of calling code.

The payoff is extensibility: the loop never changes when a new shape is added — `Pentagon` just needs to implement `area()`, and the existing calling code picks it up automatically because it was never written against any specific shape.

This is the mechanism, not just a vocabulary word, behind "program to an interface, not an implementation" from the Abstraction topic — polymorphism is what makes that advice actually work at runtime.

These two are both called "polymorphism" but resolve at completely different times, which is exactly why interviewers ask about the distinction.

| | Overloading (compile-time) | Overriding (runtime) |
|---|---|---|
| Where it happens | Multiple methods, same name, same class, different parameter types | A subclass replaces a base class's instance method |
| Resolved by | The compiler, using the argument types at the call site | The runtime, using the object's actual class |
| Requires inheritance? | No | Yes |
| Also called | Static/ad-hoc polymorphism | Dynamic polymorphism |

**How to decide which is in play:** if resolution depends only on what you *wrote* at the call site (which overload matches these argument types), it's compile-time; if it depends on what the object *actually is* at runtime, it's runtime polymorphism.

slides.sectionTitle: How dynamic dispatch actually works: vtables/method tables
slides.markdown:
Runtime polymorphism isn't magic — most languages implement it with a **virtual method table** (vtable): each class gets one table listing, for every overridable method, the actual function address to run for that class. Every object of that class carries a hidden pointer to its class's vtable.

When you call `shape.area()`, the runtime doesn't decide at compile time which `area()` to run — it follows the object's vtable pointer, looks up the `area` slot, and jumps to whatever address is stored there. A `Circle` object's vtable has `Circle.area` in that slot; a `Square` object's vtable has `Square.area` in the same slot.

This is also why virtual calls cost a small amount more than direct calls — one extra pointer indirection through the vtable — and why languages that skip it for non-virtual methods (like C++'s default) get slightly faster non-polymorphic calls.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a vtable lookup resolving a call at runtime
slides.markdown:
A `Shape` reference holding a `Circle` object carries a hidden pointer to `Circle`'s vtable. Calling `shape.area()` follows that pointer, finds the `area` slot in `Circle`'s vtable, and jumps to `Circle.area`'s actual code — never touching `Square`'s or `Triangle`'s vtables at all.

Swap the object for a `Square` (same `Shape`-typed variable) and the same call site now follows a different vtable pointer to a different slot's address — same source line, different code executed, purely because the underlying object changed.

slides.sectionTitle: Parametric polymorphism/generics as a third kind
slides.markdown:
**Parametric polymorphism** — generics in Java/C#, templates in C++ — lets a single class or function work over any type, parameterized rather than tied to one concrete type. `List<T>` is one implementation that works identically for `List<String>`, `List<Integer>`, or `List<Car>`, without `List` needing to know or care what `T` is.

This is a genuinely different mechanism from overriding or overloading: there's no inheritance hierarchy and no compile-time method selection — the same code is reused verbatim across types, with the compiler enforcing type safety (`list.add("text")` fails to compile on a `List<Integer>`).

The three kinds together cover the full picture: overriding varies behavior by an object's runtime type, overloading varies it by argument types at compile time, and generics reuse one implementation across types without varying behavior at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a polymorphic `Shape.area()` call resolved at runtime
Pitfall: overload-resolution surprises — the "wrong" overload picked at compile time
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Overload resolution picks the overload that matches the argument's actual runtime type, just like overriding does."

**Why it's wrong:** overload resolution happens at **compile time**, based on the *declared* type of the argument expression — not the runtime type of the object it happens to hold. Calling `print(shape)` where `shape` is declared as `Shape` but actually holds a `Circle`, against overloads `print(Shape)` and `print(Circle)`, always calls `print(Shape)` — the compiler only sees the declared type, and picks the best match for that.

**Correct model:** overload resolution and override resolution answer different questions at different times — overloads are chosen by the compiler from the declared type; overrides are chosen by the runtime from the actual object. Mixing up which one applies is a common source of "why did the wrong method run" bugs.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: calling overridable methods from a constructor
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Calling an overridable method from the base class constructor is fine — it'll just run whatever the actual object's version is, same as any other call."

**Why it's wrong:** it does dispatch to the subclass's override — that's exactly the problem. Base constructors run before the subclass's own constructor body, so the override executes while the subclass's own fields are still at their default (often `null` or `0`), not yet set up. A `Vehicle` constructor calling an overridable `getDefaultSpeed()`, overridden by `SportsCar` to return `topSpeed * 0.9`, runs that override before `SportsCar`'s constructor has set `topSpeed` — silently producing `0`, not a sensible default.

**Correct model:** never call an overridable method from a constructor. If subclass-specific setup logic is genuinely needed, do it in a separate initialization method called *after* construction completes, once every field in the hierarchy is guaranteed to be set.

slides.sectionTitle: Why polymorphism is what makes the Open/Closed Principle possible
slides.markdown:
The Open/Closed Principle says code should be open to extension but closed to modification — you should be able to add new behavior without editing existing, tested code. Polymorphism is the concrete mechanism that makes this achievable: a function written against a `Shape` interface never needs to change when `Pentagon` is added, because the existing call site dispatches to whichever `area()` the new object provides.

Without polymorphism, adding a new shape would mean editing a big `if (shape instanceof Circle) ... else if (shape instanceof Square) ...` chain everywhere shapes are handled — every addition touches, and risks breaking, existing code.

The connection is worth stating explicitly in an interview: Open/Closed isn't an abstract design ideal, it's a direct, practical consequence of relying on runtime polymorphism instead of type-checking branches.
